To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of evidence in policy is inevitably ideological and that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders must be included in genuine dialogue about the evidence that will be used to inform policy.
the evidence-based paradigm in Indigenous affairs is not a panacea for the problems of Indigenous disadvantage.

the question: how can evidence-based policy be used to achieve positive social change in Indigenous policy?
the ways in which Aboriginal people are able to influence the development and implementation of policies that directly impact on their lives and communities.
the role of evidence in Indigenous policy making.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders have a voice, but not necessarily a say.
the evidence-based policy framework is not a neutral, value-free process and that it is not a ‘one size fits all’ solution to policy problems.
evidence-based policy, while a useful tool, is not a panacea and that the Indigenous policy domain is one where it is most likely to fail.

we have been able to demonstrate that the evidence-based policy approach to Indigenous policy is not as simple as it is often presented, and that there are a number of complexities that need to be taken into account in order to make it work effectively.

the evidence-based policy framework is not sufficient to address Indigenous disadvantage.
